metadata.title: TMUA early specimen · Paper 2
metadata.description: Worked steps, progressive hints and reviewed follow-up questions.

matches.rationale: The shared step is interpreting centre and radius in the standard circle equation. The original must first normalise and complete squares; the candidate is already in standard form and adds coordinate centre distance and a boundary-gap calculation, so it does not itself test completing the square.

Prerequisite transfer: determine a circle centre and radius from geometric information and carry them through transformations. The original first completes two squares; the candidate obtains its centre from a diameter, so square completion is not tested again.
Uses the radius and centre distance in internal and external tangency. It extends circle interpretation to cases rather than repeating square completion.
The same radical-quotient structure is simplified to powers before differentiating and evaluating the gradient.
An expanded quadratic divided by a fractional power again becomes a short power-rule calculation.
Another official radical-denominator derivative tests termwise simplification and negative fractional exponents.
Identifies a lost sign when taking a square root, the same non-reversibility behind the specimen’s extra root.

Both audit whether squaring or reversing a square preserves the original sign restrictions and solution set. In the original, squaring an equation admits an extraneous root; in the candidate, reversing a squared inequality discards a possible negative branch.
Audits a solution for a different loss of equivalence: division removes a zero-factor solution. This contrasts adding and losing candidates.
Directly tests which proposed counterexamples have a true antecedent and a false conclusion.
A proposed composite example only works after checking the required digit-pattern hypothesis, matching the vowel-card eligibility check.
Checks both eligibility and failure of a conclusion for proposed counterexamples, with more arithmetic than the card example.
Combines exponential factors and converts the resulting equation to a logarithm using the same exponent interpretation.
Uses logarithm definitions to turn simultaneous log conditions into algebra, adding domain checks to the basic power-log conversion.
Treats logarithms as quantities obeying linear relations, then converts back to powers to obtain the required logarithm.

Both use independent interval bounds to establish an extreme, with endpoint inclusion checked. The original approaches an upper bound for a quotient by increasing its positive numerator and reducing its positive denominator; the candidate maximises an absolute product. This practises bound selection, not rounding, and no shared assessed-concept ID is claimed.
Maximises a positive reciprocal by minimising its denominator, reinforcing why a smaller positive denominator increases the quotient. The range comes from an exponential rather than rounding.

The candidate separates a bound valid for every admissible input from an equality that would require separate extrema to occur together. This transfers the original need to distinguish an upper bound from its attainment; it does not rehearse significant-figure intervals or division of positive measurements.
sharedKnowledge: Verify a bound over all allowed inputs

matches.rationale: Uses a vertex and one known point to determine a graph’s equation. It reinforces checking exact points instead of trusting the overall sketch.
Distinguishes graph transformations through an exact landmark, the vertex, rather than through visual shape alone.
Uses crossing points and direction to compare exponential graphs. The shared move is extracting exact landmark constraints before selecting a graph relationship.
Converts intersecting arithmetic progressions into a common subsequence and a modular remainder; it extends the same integer-residue reasoning.
Tests divisibility and parity claims about an integer AP with a fixed sum, requiring every integer condition to remain in force.
Tests an arithmetic-sum property through integer parameter conditions and counterexamples, extending the specimen’s exact divisibility criterion.

Disprove a universal inequality by choosing a permitted input that makes its conclusion fail. This practises the one-exception part of negating an all-input statement; it does not repeat the combined every-day and at-least-once wording.

Fixes a real input before choosing an existential witness and tests the available output range, including any exceptional coefficient cases. This transfers the some-versus-every distinction to an algebraic existence question.

Prerequisite transfer: refute an all-input claim by one permitted failure. The candidate supplies numerical inequalities; it practises the one-exception part of the original negation, not the combined every-day and at-least-once statement.
Selects an exponential-function graph from exact limits and monotonicity, the same recognition strategy as the variable-base logarithm.

Uses one-sided endpoint behaviour and an exact interior landmark to distinguish graphs of variable powers. It adds trigonometry while retaining the original strategy of matching numerical behaviours to a graph.
Simplifies nested logarithms and uses the shared input range and intersection landmark to order the two functions.

Both compare a positive surd expression with exact rational bounds. The original uses 0<sqrt(2)-1<1 in a mixed-number comparison; the candidate uses sign bounds to choose the principal roots of binomial squares, then adds them. This is a limited exact-surd comparison transfer with an additional square-recognition step.
sharedKnowledge: bound positive surds using rational squares

matches.rationale: Uses exact trigonometric values with quadrant signs; this specifically repairs the sign-sensitive standard-angle comparison in the original.
Proves an exponential comparison from ordered exponents without numerical approximation. It extends bounding individual options to a universal inequality.
Evaluates an unexpanded polynomial at the divisor’s root to obtain its remainder directly.
Uses two prescribed polynomial roots to form parameter equations, contrasting the zero-remainder case with the original nonzero remainder.
Starts from a factor-theorem input, then divides and factors the remaining polynomial. This builds on evaluation as the gateway to division.

Both enumerate complete permutations subject to position or relative-order restrictions. The runner question fixes forced positions and counts orders; the password question first enumerates excluded-position assignments, then additionally designs distinguishing feedback. Only the constrained-permutation enumeration is shared.
sharedKnowledge: Both enumerate complete permutations subject to position or relative-order restrictions. The runner question fixes forced positions and counts orders; the password question first enumerates excluded-position assignments, then additionally designs distinguishing feedback. Only the constrained-permutation enumeration is shared.

matches.rationale: Uses turning-point heights to derive a cubic root-count range, then distinguishes a sufficient subset from an exact condition.
Propagates a negative ordering through products and quotients, requiring the same attention to sign reversals.
Proves a universal inequality and refutes other proposed inequalities with permitted numerical choices.
Tests whether proposed operations on simultaneous inequalities are valid, using counterexamples when a sign condition is missing.
Computes a short recurrence until a previous state returns, then aligns a large index with the verified four-cycle.
Finds eventual cycles of parity-dependent recurrences; it adds an initial transient to the original periodic recurrence.
Tracks partial sums across a short trigonometric cycle and groups complete blocks before treating the remaining positions.

Keep the real and integer domains attached to their quantifiers and distinguish a single witness from a witness chosen after each input. This directly reinforces the order and scope of the quantifiers before negating a nested definition.
sharedKnowledge: Preserve the domain of each variable

matches.rationale: Negates a universal-existential prime-divisibility definition while retaining the eligible member and other-member restriction.
Negates three nested integer quantifiers and a primality predicate without changing their order or domains.

Both identify the median through sorted entries and check which repetitions the question permits. The original bounds an odd-list median under a mean and range constraint; the follow-up checks median membership for odd and even list lengths. This is a median-definition and admissible-example prerequisite, not practice of the original extremal argument.
Optimises a range under integer mean and median constraints, combining a bound with a feasible construction as in the extremal specimen median.

Prerequisite transfer: apply input and output substitutions in the stated order. The candidate transforms a particular quadratic and checks its vertex; it does not repeat the original polynomial zero-set reflection.
Prerequisite transfer: interpret a reflected input as an identity holding for every real input. The candidate locates an axis of symmetry rather than proving a reflected polynomial zero set.
Proves that -f(-x) has precisely the reflected original zeros, matching the specimen’s root-sign reversal directly.
Checks all possible values of a shared parameter under an exactly-one-true condition, retaining only consistent truth assignments.

Both use implications between statements to eliminate inconsistent whole truth assignments. The candidate has a unique true option among universal threshold rules; the original includes self-referential truth counts and a name fact, so the transfer is the dependency/consistency operation rather than an identical truth table.
sharedKnowledge: Both use implications between statements to eliminate inconsistent whole truth assignments. The candidate has a unique true option among universal threshold rules; the original includes self-referential truth counts and a name fact, so the transfer is the dependency/consistency operation rather than an identical truth table.

matches.rationale: Both assign truth values to all interdependent statements in one shared configuration, split exhaustive cases and reject any assignment inconsistent with its own truth count. The grid task additionally negates neighbour quantifiers and uses geometric symmetry; the other question uses a common urn count or an unknown factual atom and speaker-count assertions. The shared operation is whole-configuration truth consistency.
sharedKnowledge: Both assign truth values to all interdependent statements in one shared configuration, split exhaustive cases and reject any assignment inconsistent with its own truth count. The grid task additionally negates neighbour quantifiers and uses geometric symmetry; the other question uses a common urn count or an unknown factual atom and speaker-count assertions. The shared operation is whole-configuration truth consistency.

review.source: Official question papers and official worked answers; archived question-bank lessons
scopeNotes: The official archive has only one rounded-measurement error-bound question: Q6 follow-ups train endpoint choice, reciprocal bounds and joint attainment; they are marked transfer rather than exact rounding matches.
There is only one runner partial-order counting question: Q13 follow-ups train constrained counting and permutations; two are coefficient-selection transfers.
review.quality: Every link was reviewed for the named shared knowledge; a transfer label distinguishes supporting skills from a close structural match.

followupGaps.reason: Retained the constrained-permutation follow-up. Removed two coefficient-selection tasks: general counting alone does not rehearse the required runner-order restrictions. No closer replacements yet reviewed. Frozen editions unchanged.
